prerequisites: Identify the audience and purpose of a communication.
Explain an idea with relevant examples.
goals: Plan and deliver a clear formal presentation.
Listen to questions and respond appropriately.
Understand the optional endorsement’s separate all-criteria assessment.

sections.title: A separate, optional spoken endorsement
paragraphs: The optional 4EB1/E endorsement develops formal speaking, listening and responses to questions. It is assessed by the centre and reported separately as Not Classified, Pass, Merit or Distinction. It carries no numerical marks and does not add marks to the 100-mark written examination.

Discuss participation and the arrangements with your teacher. Website rehearsal, a transcript or an automatically generated score cannot award the official endorsement. These lessons offer original preparation activities; they do not reproduce a candidate assessment or replace a teacher’s judgement.

example.question: A student has a written-exam score and a strong presentation. Should the teacher add presentation marks to the written total?
steps: Keep the written examination and spoken endorsement separate.
Report the endorsement through its own grade, without inventing a numeric conversion.
example.explanation: Understand the two distinct assessment purposes before planning practice.

practice.question: Does the endorsement change the written-paper mark maximum?
practice.answer: No. It is separately reported and has no numerical marks.
practice.explanation: Understand the two distinct assessment purposes before planning practice.

sections.title: Choose a purpose, audience and presentation form
paragraphs: Prepare a speech or talk followed by audience questions, or a formal debate or dialogue such as an interview with prepared extended responses and subsequent questions. Choose a clear purpose: explain an issue, persuade listeners to consider a proposal, or explore a reasoned position.

The audience must include the teacher. Agree its size and composition with the teacher. A teacher-only presentation should still be designed for a potentially wider audience, such as a broadcast interview. Address what listeners already know, why the subject matters and which terms need explanation.

example.question: Plan a talk recommending a quieter school study area to students and staff.
steps: Purpose: recommend a practical improvement.
Audience: students and staff with different concerns about space and supervision.
Form: a reasoned talk with questions afterwards.
example.explanation: Audience choices shape content and explanation, not just the greeting.

practice.question: How could a teacher-only interview still address a wider audience?
practice.answer: Frame questions and explanations for viewers who need the topic introduced, rather than relying on private classroom knowledge.
practice.explanation: Audience choices shape content and explanation, not just the greeting.

sections.title: Build a clear structure within the time limit
paragraphs: The prepared presentation should last no longer than ten minutes. Confirm with the teacher how the question period is organised and rehearse the whole planned format. A useful original structure is an opening purpose, a small number of linked ideas, supporting examples, and a conclusion that returns to the purpose.

Signpost the progression in language listeners can follow. Develop fewer ideas well instead of racing through many unrelated points. Use brief cue notes and practise transitions; a memorised script alone does not show whether the audience can follow the reasoning.

example.question: Outline a presentation arguing for a school book swap.
steps: Introduce the problem of books being unused.
Explain access and waste benefits using relevant examples.
Consider collection and organisation challenges.
Conclude with a workable proposal and rehearse its timing.
example.explanation: Editing the content helps preserve clarity; simply speaking faster may make it harder to understand.

practice.question: A rehearsal takes twelve minutes. What should change?
practice.answer: Cut or combine less relevant material and rehearse again until the prepared presentation meets the ten-minute maximum.
practice.explanation: Editing the content helps preserve clarity; simply speaking faster may make it harder to understand.

sections.title: Speak clearly in a formal setting
paragraphs: All graded levels require an audible, intelligible performance and spoken Standard English appropriate to the formal setting. The source describes intelligibility and suitable language; it does not require imitating a particular accent.

Rehearse at a measured pace, pronounce key terms clearly and use pauses to separate ideas. Check that a listener at the back can hear. Choose vocabulary you understand and can explain. A sophisticated word that is used inaccurately may obscure the idea.

example.question: A speaker rushes an important definition and then uses unexplained jargon. How can the delivery improve?
steps: Pause before the definition and explain it in clear language.
Give a concrete example.
Ask a practice listener whether the explanation was audible and understandable.
example.explanation: Assess the communication evidence rather than treating accent as a grading shortcut.

practice.question: Does an unusual accent by itself show failure to use spoken Standard English?
practice.answer: No. The specified general requirements concern intelligibility and language generally appropriate to the formal setting.
practice.explanation: Assess the communication evidence rather than treating accent as a grading shortcut.

sections.title: Develop ideas that engage the audience
paragraphs: Move beyond naming an opinion by explaining the reasoning, giving relevant examples and considering a meaningful challenge. Distinguish an observation, an inference and a claim that needs supporting evidence. A presentation on a debated issue can acknowledge uncertainty without losing its purpose.

Vocabulary, organisation and audience engagement work together. At higher levels the source expects challenging or sophisticated ideas, suitable vocabulary and effective ways to engage listeners. There is no official rule awarding one mark for each rhetorical device. Use questions, contrasts or examples only when they improve the communication.

example.question: Improve the claim “Every school should replace textbooks with tablets.”
steps: Explain the proposed learning benefit.
Consider cost, access, distraction and reliability.
Use sourced evidence if available and distinguish it from a personal example.
Refine the recommendation to address the strongest objection.
example.explanation: A strategy matters because of its effect on the listener, not because it appears on a checklist.

practice.question: Why does adding five rhetorical questions not guarantee a higher grade?
practice.answer: The endorsement assesses the whole performance against all criteria; a device count does not establish reasoning, audience engagement or effective responses.
practice.explanation: A strategy matters because of its effect on the listener, not because it appears on a checklist.

sections.title: Listen before answering questions and feedback
paragraphs: The presentation includes responding to questions or feedback. Listen to the whole question, identify its main concern, then answer directly. If the question is unclear, request clarification. If you do not know a fact, say so and explain what you would need to establish it.

A fuller response can give a reason, an example and an appropriate elaboration while staying relevant. Prepare for objections, limitations and requests for clarification rather than only rehearsing friendly questions. The source distinguishes straightforward appropriate responses, formal responses with some detail, and perceptive responses with further ideas where appropriate.

example.question: After a book-swap proposal, a listener asks how damaged books will be handled.
steps: Acknowledge the practical concern.
Propose clear acceptance criteria and explain who checks them.
Consider alternatives for books unsuitable for the swap.
example.explanation: Relevant detail grows from listening; a prepared speech does not answer every question automatically.

practice.question: What should you do if a question has two parts?
practice.answer: Identify both parts, answer each in turn and check that the response addressed the listener’s actual concern.
practice.explanation: Relevant detail grows from listening; a prepared speech does not answer every question automatically.

sections.title: Understand the all-criteria grading rule
paragraphs: The endorsement uses an all-criteria rule. To earn a level, the performance must meet every requirement for that level. The assessment record also requires all criteria for preceding levels where applicable. Strength in one area does not compensate arithmetically for a missing criterion elsewhere.

Pass includes straightforward ideas, an attempt at organisation and audience awareness, and appropriate straightforward responses. Merit develops challenging ideas with a range of vocabulary, clear audience-suited organisation, achievement of purpose and formal responses in some detail. Distinction develops sophisticated ideas and vocabulary, effective audience-engagement strategies, achievement of purpose and perceptive responses with elaboration where appropriate. Audibility and suitable spoken Standard English remain general requirements.

example.question: A speaker gives an engaging talk but no evidence of listening and responding is assessed. Can presentation strength alone establish Distinction?
steps: Check the listening/response criteria as well as the presentation.
Do not average strengths into a grade.
Arrange appropriate evidence under the centre’s assessment conditions.
example.explanation: A rehearsal checklist helps identify gaps but is not the official assessment outcome.

practice.question: Can six practice checkmarks be converted into an official percentage grade?
practice.answer: No. The official levels require all applicable criteria, assessed by the centre; this site does not award an endorsement grade.
practice.explanation: A rehearsal checklist helps identify gaps but is not the official assessment outcome.

sections.title: Rehearse, review and agree the assessment arrangements
paragraphs: For preparation, give the talk to a willing listener, invite questions and ask for specific feedback on audibility, clarity, structure and relevance. Review one weakness at a time and repeat the rehearsal. If a recording is useful, agree consent and how it will be stored; this site does not record or upload your voice or video.

Teachers organise assessment records and the required recording sample under Pearson’s current instructions. The specification distinguishes the sample from recording every student and gives separate rules for centres with thirty or fewer students and larger centres. Confirm the current submission arrangements with the centre; a learner should not submit an informal website recording as an official assessment.

Keep the work your own and identify sources used for factual claims. Ask the teacher about permitted assistance and declarations. Use the official assessment record for formal evidence and original practice activities here for rehearsal.

example.question: Create a plan for two useful practice sessions.
steps: First session: check timing, audibility and structure with a practice listener.
Invite questions and record written feedback.
Revise the weakest explanation.
Second session: rehearse with unfamiliar questions and check improvement.
example.explanation: The learner’s rehearsal and the centre’s official evidence have different roles.

practice.question: Which organisation decides the official assessment conditions and recording submission?
practice.answer: Your centre follows Pearson’s current instructions and the official assessment record. These practice activities do not make a formal entry or submission.
practice.explanation: The learner’s rehearsal and the centre’s official evidence have different roles.
